newsitem.title: PERU: Peru peace brokers on upbeat mood despite snag.
newsitem.headline: Peru peace brokers on upbeat mood despite snag.

text.p: Peace brokers in Peru's 15-week hostage siege said on Sunday they believed that despite a low point in negotiations a bloodless way out would be found.
"We are working together towards a quick, peaceful solution," Canadian ambassador Anthony Vincent told reporters.

Vincent, Peruvian Archbishop Juan Cipriani and Red Cross representative Michel Minnig form a peace guarantors team seeking a negotiated end to 103 days of captivity for 72 hostages held by Marxist rebels at the Japanese ambassador's residence.

Cipriani said after separate meetings with government representative Domingo Palermo and rebel leaders: "The talks have not broken down. We are continually talking to the MRTA (rebels) and the government. "We are trying to move as fast as possible."

Although the Easter weekend helped generate a positive atmosphere, it dissipated when both President Alberto Fujimori and Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leader Nestor Cerpa dug in their heels.

"There was a lot of speculation during Holy Week that there would be a peaceful solution, but we were conscious that we were not in the final stage, that the conditions were not right," Fujimori said in a television interview aired on Sunday.
"Naturally, we are hopeful that it will be the soonest possible, but we do not glimpse a date."

Fujimori insisted he was not ready to free any of MRTA's 450 prisoners. Their release was the main demand the rebels made after blasting their way into the residence on Dec. 17, triggering Latin America's longest hostage siege.
Cerpa said by walkie-talkie from the compound: "We still don't foresee a peaceful solution soon. The positions are still not really drawing close."

A meeting between Cerpa and Palermo that was widely expected to take place Monday or Tuesday is now unlikely to happen so soon. Although the guarantors keep them in constant touch, the two sides have not met face-to-face since March 12.
Both Fujimori and Cerpa also denied widespread speculation that the MRTA had paved the way for a deal by accepting a Cuban offer of political asylum for the 20-odd hostage-takers.
The dashed hopes after a week of upbeat mood caused the head of Peru's Roman Catholic church to lash out at the MRTA captors in his Easter Sunday mass.
"They have missed the chance to show that they respect the will of the majority," Cardinal Augusto Vargas Alzamora said.

"The people are asking them to come out and instead of being generous they use arms to maintain the situation. I am saddened that Mr. Cerpa Cartolini has said that there remains much time for this to fix itself," he added. "He should learn from God and not feel superior."

It was a gloomy Easter for the hostages, who have also spent Christmas and New Year's in captivity. They held a mass and got chocolate Easter eggs and fresh fruit with their usual daily supply of meals brought in by the Red Cross.
Among the captives are the ambassadors of Japan and Bolivia, Fujimori's brother, Pedro, two cabinet ministers, military officers and Japanese businessmen and diplomats.
In Rome, Pope John Paul offered them a special thought in his "Urbi et Orbi" Easter message to the world. "May they finally gain the freedom they ardently long for," he said.
Fujimori said a special committee would continue to study pardons for Peruvians unjustly jailed on terrorism or treason charges for alleged ties to Peru's two leftist rebel groups.

Recommendations by the panel formed before the MRTA stormed the residence led to about 100 pardons. Fujimori said the committee would propose more pardons but insisted the siege had "nothing to do with the release of those unjustly condemned."
He also said his government was working to improve jail conditions, another main concern of rebels who complain that their comrades are condemned to slow deaths in virtual "tombs."
